notes.text:
TEST 1 - RUN THE PORTABLE WORKFLOW
Run the workflow on the supplied cleanup sample. PASS: its third channel becomes a clean 3D mask, one isolated 19-voxel speck is removed, one enclosed cavity is filled, and the final label image contains four separate objects. The workflow remains usable on a CPU-only computer.

TEST 2 - UNDERSTAND CHANNEL EXTRACTION
On a CPU-to-GPU boundary, CPU Extract Channel can select this one ZYX channel before upload. When Extract Channel itself joins an already resident GPU segment, it makes a no-copy view of the full CZYX GPU allocation. That keeps work connected, but is not automatically the fastest choice at the first node.

TEST 3 - CHECK GPU ELIGIBILITY
This example asks for Prefer GPU. On a qualified CUDA setup, the visible float32 Preserve conversion lets the filter and later supported nodes form one GPU segment. PASS: VIPP reports what actually ran. GPU eligible is not guaranteed: data, memory, environment, and policy checks can still choose CPU.

TEST 4 - REVIEW THE THRESHOLD
The value 18180.26953125 sits midway inside a wide gap in this deterministic sample, more than 433 intensity units from every blurred pixel value. PASS: the mask contains 2428 foreground voxels before cleanup. This margin makes CPU/GPU comparison clear for this example; it is not a recommended threshold for unrelated images.

TEST 5 - VERIFY MASK CLEANUP
Remove Small Objects uses an exact 22-voxel minimum, so the isolated 19-voxel speck disappears while the four larger objects remain. Fill Holes then restores 31 enclosed 3D background voxels. PASS: cleanup remains boolean, preserves ZYX metadata, and the final component volumes are 685, 599, 595, and 561 voxels.

TEST 6 - READ TRANSFERS AND FALLBACK HONESTLY
With only the final label output retained, a fully eligible run can cross the CPU/GPU boundary once in each direction. Previewing, branching to, or retaining an intermediate result can add a download. If any GPU gate fails, VIPP explains the fallback and completes the same workflow on CPU.
